surfaces.part: meat display interior with glass reflection

answer.evidence: Rows 2-5 form a light glass top band that brightens toward the front (L 166 to 246). It ends in a dark front-edge line at row 6, which counts as the top surface under evidence (a). Below it the front face runs from about row 7 to row 29. It shows the meat shelf interior behind glass (rows 7-19), a shelf edge at row 20, and a red front panel (rows 22-28). The top band is only 4 rows and the interior is drawn face-on, so the read is borderline. The edge line and the band's gradient still favor a top surface over a plain cornice.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are fine: 15 visible tones per tile against 17 for the cheese stall and 20 for the well, 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outline is tinted rather than a pure black line. By eye the piece is weaker than that suggests. It is a wide, low rectangle built from flat horizontal bands (a pale top, a dark navy stripe, a red stripe and a pale bottom), each with only about 2-3 lightness steps. The references use 5-6 steps per material. There is no tile-by-tile highlighting, no grain, and no visible meat or goods inside, unlike the cheese stall with its awning, shelves and wares. The detail that exists is mostly stripe edges and a few dots, and it reads as a flat sticker-like panel rather than a shaded prop. Shading depth and object richness are below the Beodeul bar, so I fail it on doubt despite the decent tone count.

surfaces.part: glass window with meat trays (front view)
front base panel (white and red bands)

answer.evidence: Rows 2-5 form a light gradient band (L 166 to 246) across the full 48px width. Row 5 is the lightest row and works as the front-edge line, and row 6 is a dark shadow line directly under it. That is a top surface 4 rows tall, per evidence (a). Below it the front face runs from about row 7 to row 29. It holds the glass window with meat trays seen face-on (rows 7-19), a ledge line at row 20, and a white and red base panel (rows 22-29). No side face is drawn. The top is thin but it has a clear edge line and shadow, so it is more than a 1-2 row rim.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are acceptable: 15 visible tones per tile against 17-20 for the stall and well, 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outline is tinted rather than near-black. By eye, though, the piece reads as a flat horizontal striped panel. It has a pale top band, red and white stripes, and a dark navy base. Each material carries only about 3 lightness steps, where the cheese stall and well carry 5-6. It shows no meat, no wood frame or grain, no awning scallops and no per-item shading. The red and white bands look like banded fills with little grain, and the whole piece is thinner and more sticker-like than the cheese stall next to it. A careful artist would not accept it beside the reference without more form and texture, and when in doubt the rule is to fail.

The meat trays are drawn in elevation, so they are not contents seen from above. The top reading is modest and leans on the band and edge line alone. There is no receding side face.

The tinted outline and lack of flat fills keep it from failing outright, but a careful artist would not accept it next to the references.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are acceptable. By eye it is weaker than the stall-cheese and well references. It reads as a flat horizontal strip of stacked bands (white, dark navy, red, white) with a thin outline.
